reason: The sources provide over 20 cross-referenced facts detailing the 13-day siege, the rapid 90-minute final massacre, and the specific names of survivors and commanders.
story: In February 1836, nearly 200 Texian volunteers were trapped inside the crumbling Alamo mission. For 13 days, they watched as a blood-red flag—a signal of 'no quarter'—waved from a nearby cathedral, promising that no prisoners would be taken. Under freezing rain and a constant artillery barrage, the defenders, including Jim Bowie and Davy Crockett, sent desperate couriers to beg for reinforcements that never arrived. In the early hours of March 6, the Mexican Army launched a silent dawn assault. The carnage was swift; the battle was over in just 90 minutes. William B. Travis fell at the north wall, and a bedridden Bowie was killed in his room. Only a few women, children, and a slave were spared to spread the terrifying news. Though Santa Anna burned the bodies of the fallen on massive pyres, their death galvanized an army that would win independence just six weeks later.
angle: The legendary 13-day stand ended in a brutal massacre that lasted only 90 minutes, leaving nearly every defender dead before the sun was fully up.

claims.claim: The Battle of the Alamo took place from February 23 to March 6, 1836.
The garrison was led by co-commanders William B. Travis and James Bowie.
The Mexican forces were commanded by General Antonio López de Santa Anna.
Mexican troops raised a blood-red flag signifying that no quarter would be given to survivors.
William B. Travis responded to the demand for surrender by firing an 18-pounder cannon.
James Bowie became severely ill during the siege and was confined to his bed.
On February 24, Travis wrote a famous letter 'To the People of Texas & All Americans in the World' pleading for aid.
Thirty-two reinforcements from Gonzales successfully entered the Alamo on March 1.
The final assault began around 5:30 a.m. on March 6, 1836.
The actual fighting during the final assault lasted approximately 90 minutes.
William B. Travis was among the first to die, shot at the north wall.
Texian bodies were stacked and burned on funeral pyres after the battle.
Susanna Dickinson and her daughter Angelina were among the few noncombatant survivors spared by Santa Anna.
Mexican casualties in the battle are estimated to be between 400 and 600 killed or wounded.
News of the defeat sparked the 'Runaway Scrape,' a mass exodus of Texian settlers fleeing eastward.
Texians defeated Santa Anna at the Battle of San Jacinto on April 21, 1836, while shouting 'Remember the Alamo!'
The battle at San Jacinto lasted only 18 minutes.
Santa Anna was captured the day after the Battle of San Jacinto.
The Alamo was originally established as a Spanish mission around 1718.

disputed: The story of Travis drawing a line in the sand is considered legend and lacks primary source evidence; a script should attribute this to tradition or leave it out.
Accounts of David Crockett's death vary between him dying in combat or being among a small group executed after surrendering; a script should state that historians disagree.
The exact number of Texian defenders varies between 182 and 257; a script should use 'nearly 200'.

Specific details of Jim Bowie's death are conflicting, with some saying he died fighting from his bed and others saying he was bayoneted while unconscious; a script should attribute these as 'conflicting accounts'.
